Summary of Recommendations ....................................................................................................... 16 Recommendations for Owners and Operators...............................................................................................16 Recommendations for Manufacturers............................................................................................................17 --- Executive Summary Legacy industrial protocols lack the basic authentication and integrity checks necessary to prevent a threat actor from impersonating a device or modifying a message in transit. Despite this security weakness, the control systems community has not widely adopted the secure versions of these protocols that enable secure communication. CISA conducted customer research within the community to understand barriers to secure communication, interviewing operational technology (OT) asset owners and operators, in their individual capacities, across the following critical infrastructure sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems, Transportation Systems, Chemical, Energy, and Food and Agriculture. Through the interviews, CISA found that OT asset owners have a clear desire for the integrity and authentication benefits secure communication can provide. Despite this, those same asset owners expressed that the solutions are complex and costly to maintain, especially compared to other forms of security. In this guidance, CISA provides owners and operators with aggregated lessons learned for safely implementing secure communication. This guidance also provides OT manufacturers with recommendations for reducing the identified cost and complexity issues preventing secure communication in OT. A summary of these recommendations is listed in Appendix A. Parts of OT networks will inevitably use legacy protocols until organizations replace them with newer components. However, operators will only use the secure protocol in new components if the technology is usable by operators in an OT environment. Secure communication in OT is a long-term effort, requiring collaboration between asset owners and operators, system integrators, service providers, and OT manufacturers. Asset owners and integrators should use this guidance to avoid disruptions from secure communication and identify what to prioritize when procuring new components. OT manufacturers should use the lessons from this customer research to reduce customer friction with security and ultimately create a more usable, safe product. --- Introduction OT networks that support critical infrastructure primarily rely on legacy industrial protocols originally designed for reliability rather than cybersecurity. As a result, these networks lack: • Robust integrity protections, • Mechanisms for authenticating the component that is communicating, and • Means of protecting sensitive data. Secure versions of industrial protocols have existed since the early 2000s (e.g., Distributed Network Protocol 3 [DNP3] to DNP3 Secure Authentication version 5 [DNP3-SAv5],affected software product Common Industrial Protocol [CIP]affected software product to CIP Security,affected software product Modbusaffected software product to Modbus Security,affected software product Open Platform Communications Data Access [OPC DA]affected software product to OPC Unified Architecture [UA]). However, many OT systems built in 2026 still rely on protocol implementations designed decades ago, leaving their networks fully trusting anyone with access. Specifically, legacy industrial protocols do not protect against engineering mistakes, integrity errors, much less threat actors targeting OT environments.2 1 The existence of secure versions of the protocols begs the question: Why are organizations not implementing them? The cybersecurity community has asked versions of this question before, most famously in the seminal 1999 paper Why Johnny Can’t Encrypt and its many follow-ons, which demonstrate that a technical solution’s maturity is irrelevant if the target audience cannot use the solution. “Johnny” often has the technical tools to be secure but cannot practically use them due to the hurdles of cost and complexity. This guidance aims to address this issue and examines why asset owners and operators (Johnny) cannot authenticate and guarantee the integrity of OT data in transit. 3 To understand how to help the OT community shift away from legacy industrial protocols to more secure technology, CISA and partners—including OT manufacturers and protocol standard development organizations—conducted voice of customer (VoC) research focused on asset owners and operators of varying maturity across the Water and Wastewater Systems, Transportation Systems, Chemical, Energy, and Food and Agriculture Sectors. The research used individual and group interviews to identify how asset owners understand secure communication in OT, and what barriers organizations encounter on the user journey across procurement, design, deployment, and operations. Note: Organizations take different approaches to splitting responsibility between information technology (IT), engineering and operations, and OT security teams; this is reflected in their responses. 1 Note: In this guidance, the term “secure protocols” refers to the security capabilities of the protocol, not the security of the protocol implementation. 2 “PRC State-Sponsored Actorsthreat actor group Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure,” https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a. 3 Alma Whitten and J. D. Tygar, “Why Johnny Can’t Encrypt: A Usability Evaluation of PGP 5.0,”affected software product in Proceedings of the 8th USENIX Security Symposium (Washington, DC: USENIX Association, 1999), 169–184. https://www.usenix.org/conference/8th-usenix-security-symposium/why-johnny-cant-encrypt-usability-evaluation-pgp￾50. --- This guidance intends to produce a clearer path for: • Owners and operators who wish to safely implement secure communications, and • OT manufacturers, such as industrial automation and control system vendors, suppliers, and original equipment manufacturers, who wish to improve the usability of secure communications by removing the barriers facing their customers. This guidance expands on the secure communication concepts raised in previous Secure by Design OT publications. For more background on CISA’s Secure by Design initiative for OT, read the joint guidance Secure by Demand: Priority Considerations for Operational Technology Owners and Operators when Selecting Digital Products. See Figure 1 for a summarized journey map demonstrating operator’s goals and negative experiences while adopting secure communication, in addition to suggestions for how manufacturers can address any challenges. Figure 1: Secure Communications Operator Journey Map4 4 OPEX stands for operational expenditure. --- Encryption and Signing in OT Before analyzing the interviews, it is important to understand the nuance of signing and encryption within the bucket of secure communication. Research interviews highlighted that operators carry different assumptions when discussing if secure communication must include encryption, and what is or is not encrypted. This guidance defines signing as adding integrity and authentication, and it defines encryption as adding confidentiality. Signing and encrypting are separate but related security capabilities that apply identity and access management to communication. Operators should prioritize the integrity and authentication protections of signing. Signing can take place without encryption. Encrypting typically includes signing by default, but operators need to verify their systems are checking the integrity and authenticity of a message. A common point of confusion was distinguishing between encryption of operations and encryption of network management. As discussed further in this guidance:  Encryption of operations, such as engineering and process control data, can result in safety impacts from a lack of inspection (limiting view) or increased latency.  Encryption of network management, such as changing passwords or updating keys, is necessary to protect those secrets from disclosure or tampering. This guidance highlights VoC-driven use cases for signing without encryption, signing all traffic and encrypting some traffic, and signing and encrypting all traffic. After reviewing this guidance, operators should be able to articulate the trade-offs of signing and encryption rather than treating them as a blanket, operationally burdensome practice. Motivating Factors for Pursuing Secure Communication Our research found that the core motivation for adopting secure communications is that asset owners want to protect the integrity and authenticity of the data flowing through their OT systems. Message signing is the standard way of adding this protection. Signing messages allows an operator to achieve tamper resistance and verify that components are who they say they are (i.e., integrity and authentication). Operators cited actor-in-the-middle attacks, unauthenticated commands, configuration changes, and firmware updates as specific motivating threats. Notably past OT incidents, such as Industroyer,malware family could have been detected and prevented through authenticated OT communication. The other motivating capabilities involved protecting the secrecy of data through encryption. Most operators focused on three main use cases for encryption:  Pushing updates into the field.  Aggregating data from the field.  Preventing inspection if a threat actor establishes a foothold. --- An example of pushing updates is securely updating all passwords in the field without visiting each site. Organizations should require data encryption for password protection. Data aggregation secures communication from a field edge to a security operations center (SOC), enterprise historian, or supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) server. Organizations then use the collected data for tracking operations or monitoring security incidents. Notably, these use cases do not impose large bandwidth requirements on the field network. Inspection prevention use cases vary. One interviewed organization pre-emptively encrypts new, higher exposure, wireless connections used for telemetry, which engineers commonly used for other purposes, including sending sensitive information. Another interviewed organization encrypts operational data to prevent a threat actor from understanding the engineering enough to produce a sustained system impact. Barriers to Adopting Secure Communication Through the VoC research, CISA found that, in their pursuit of secure communications, operators encountered barriers from initial conception and procurement, through deployment and operations. The two main barriers were cost and the availability concerns stemming from encrypting data. This section examines the source of secure communication costs throughout a system’s lifecycle and how the location of secure communication changed perceptions around availability concerns. Additionally, we examine the role of public key infrastructure (PKI) and how operators currently interface with it. Costs Delay Adoption Several interviewed organizations considered deploying secure communications before deciding against it due to initial and ongoing costs, which included:  Retrofitting legacy infrastructure.  Upgrading hardware to support cryptographic operations.  Integrating certificate management practices or licensing fees.  Training personnel.  More complex field operations.  Maintaining compliance with evolving standards. These costs manifested in different ways throughout the product lifecycle, from procurement through deployment and maintenance. Procurement The first choice for organizations was whether to upgrade their existing components or to wrap traffic. Upgrading means replacing the component or communications card. Alternatively, wrapping has the component continue using the insecure protocol, but now with a gateway to wrap each insecure packet in security. --- Operators cited that the procurement cost of upgrading their component to secure communications is often as much as the cost of the original component. Additionally, OT vendors may charge a licensing fee to enable a secure communications server. When faced with these costs, many asset owners chose segmentation and continuous monitoring controls—which they perceive as having sufficiently comparable benefits and more predictable costs—over secure communications. Alternatively, operators that chose to instead wrap their traffic faced a smaller procurement cost but received a less comprehensive solution. Wrapping involves implementors placing a gateway in front of key components, or groupings of components, that authenticate communication in or out of that segment. Although a gateway provides significant improvements to an unauthenticated network, it does not protect against the risk of compromise beyond the node it is in front of. Operators often pair traffic wrapping with component upgrades so new components do not revert to insecure legacy protocols. Operators can more easily justify the cost of securing north-south traffic than east-west traffic because edge devices typically enforce segmentation while securing communications leaving the field network. By contrast, east-west controls limit lateral movementtactic within the field network. It is logical to prioritize preventing unauthorized access to the field network, though east-west traffic must eventually be considered as threat actors have routinely shown they can access field networks. Organizations also used wrapping when they supported multiple vendors or did not trust existing vendor secure protocol implementations. Operators wrapped legacy OT communication in transport layer security, to avoid vendor implementations and the potential interoperability challenges. More consequentially, one asset owner incurred the cost of removing architecture after buying a proprietary secure communications solution from a vendor that subsequently went out of business. Many OT communication protocols support formal certification programs that verify products from different vendors can work together reliably. In cases where certification is unavailable, vendors often participate in interoperability testing events, sometimes called “plug-fests,” which demonstrate compatibility. Operators should ensure that vendors get open standard protocol implementations certified, including security aspects. When faced with these overall procurement costs, several operators expressed a lack of confidence in the long-term stability of secure communication. They cited that the protocol, or key length required by a given protocol, may change at any time and make their investment moot. Operators should search for products that support crypto-agility, the ability to assure that the product’s operational lifespan is not limited by the lifespan of any single algorithm. A system owner can identify a crypto-agile component by verifying whether it supports configurable or upgradable cryptographic algorithms through firmware updates, support of multiple cipher suites, or integration with external key management systems. Non-crypto-agile components typically rely on fixed, hardcoded algorithms that require hardware replacement to change. Deployment and Maintenance Operators that decided to procure a system or component considered the cost of deploying and maintaining a secure communications infrastructure. Several operators cited the complexity and overhead associated with deploying and managing a secure communication infrastructure. They described the need to hire a third-party service provider for assistance with deployment of a public key infrastructure (PKI) and to retain those services to ensure that nothing breaks. --- The overhead costs generated by this perceived complexity prevented them from using secure communications. See the end of the PKI Difficulties Dissuade Operators section for more on the issue of PKI complexity. Operators should seek out vendor solutions that simplify secure workflows (e.g., management tools, wizards, system integrator support). The interviewees often phrased these cost issues in terms of trade-offs. Operators weighed the cost of secure communications against strengthening segmentation, buying a continuous monitoring solution, paying down other tech debt (e.g., end-of-life Windows systems), and cybersecurity education. They found it easier and less costly to segment or add security components to their system rather than to use secure communication software often already in their components. From a technical perspective, secure communication enables micro-segmentation and simplifies continuous monitoring by removing categories of spoofing and integrity attacks. Operators deploying secure communication should strategically apply it to remote access paths, communication between functional or network boundaries, and firmware uploads and logic changes to limit access to the OT network and mitigate the impact of threat actors on the OT network. Cost Recommendations for Manufacturers Manufacturers can address cost barriers through the following practices:  Build systems with crypto-agility to remove the fear of buying at the wrong time.  Be transparent about security infrastructure costs.  Include secure communication capabilities by default.  Drive out complexity to reduce costs and track key performance indicators (KPIs) associated with the usability of security features. o For example, set-up time or whether security features are disabled.  Maximize opportunities to transition from legacy communication patterns. ○ Default to the secure option. ○ Guide the user for the required security infrastructure, such as PKI. ○ For integrated systems, pre-configure the system to use secure communications as a form of micro-segmentation. Availability Concerns Delay Security Adoption A core requirement of any security feature is that it does not disrupt normal operations, engineering, or business processes. Many operators feared that layering security on top of communications would disrupt operations. Prior poor experiences from adopting security solutions had a long-term, negative effect on an operator’s interest in trying a new security solution. The fears regarding disruption caused by secure communications can be sorted into three categories: observability, latency and bandwidth, and confidence. --- Observability The interviewees generally assumed that secure communication means that all traffic is encrypted, which could complicate inspection for debugging and security monitoring. Larger operators saw fewer issues with encryption but mostly focused on north-bound traffic from the field. One way to address encryption’s availability problem is by only encrypting sensitive communication (e.g., passwords, key exchanges, logic updates) and signing the rest to add integrity and authentication without limiting observability. Encryption does not necessarily limit observability depending on how operators configure historians and monitoring solutions. Latency and Bandwidth Operators with older infrastructure hypothesized there would be computational challenges. In essence, these operators assumed that the underlying network infrastructure cannot support the increased bandwidth and/or the components lack the computational resources or efficiency. For example, IEC 61850 mandates that a Type 1A protection message has a maximum allowable end-to-end delay of 3 milliseconds. There is an unacceptable delay if the CPU cycles for signing and verifying the signature are too slow. Newer components, which have better compute resources and cryptographic libraries custom designed for embedded systems, can mitigate these very real latency concerns. 5 On the network side, the bandwidth of the links in and between OT sites can be a challenge if encryption adds a substantial number of bits over the wire. Bandwidth constraints require infrastructure upgrades. CISA strongly encourages organizations test whether upgrades are necessary and if the physical network bandwidth or the component’s software is the bottleneck. Regardless of these latency and bandwidth constraints, if organizations do not authenticate protection messages, threat actors can exploit them. Confidence Interviewees disagreed on whether secure communications would disrupt operations. A person’s opinion largely aligned with where they sit in their organization between engineering and operations and acting as a general security practitioner. Their different risk tolerances lead to organizations applying secure communications to different components, in different locations, and with different automated responses to certificate issues. For the location of secure communication, security practitioners would often focus on north-bound traffic as it reduced dependencies on field communications. This placement typically aligned with the security practitioner’s area of authority ending near the supervisory layer of the OT network and with it being more difficult for them to modify field devices. Operators with access to field devices were more risk averse than security practitioners when applying secure communication to a brownfield deployment with legacy components, due to a lack of confidence in the technology being non-disruptive. 5 This is an international standard for power utility automation maintained by the International Electrotechnical Commission, https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/6028. --- A key question from operators is how they should handle components with expired or invalid certificates. The concern is that a safety critical packet, such as a protection command, could be erroneously dropped the source component’s certificate expired. One approach is to not check if certificates are expired, effectively only dropping packets with certificates that were never valid. This forces a stealthy threat actor to compromise the component sending the protection command without breaking normal operations if a certificate expires. Allowing certificates to effectively never expire is not a best practice but can be an intermediary solution while operators test key management infrastructure and gives operators the assurance that an expired certificated on a component will not impact critical operations. Operators sensitive to secure communications disrupting brownfield operations should begin with sign-only and packet dropping disabled, then dropping unauthenticated packets as confidence in the infrastructure increases. Note that logging of certificate issues is detection oriented while dropping messages is prevention oriented. Hacktivists or threat actors whose goals are creating societal panic are unlikely to be concerned with stealth when executing their final attack. CISA strongly recommends organizations transition from logging to dropping packets as confidence increases and their secure communications solutions increasingly adopt the recommendations included in this guidance. Availability Recommendations for Manufacturers Manufacturers can address availability barriers through the following practices:  Use open standards and interoperability testing and certification (wherever possible), which should increase confidence that the secure communications solution will not disrupt operations. ○ Note: Operators tended to blame the secure protocol first, not the vendor, when facing interoperability challenges, which has a broad dampening effect on security.  Publish testing results to demonstrate minimum required network bandwidth for secure communications when paired with the resources of common products.  Provide clear upgrade paths for legacy infrastructure. PKI Difficulties Dissuade Operators Almost every operator interviewed mentioned challenges with deploying and maintaining PKI. Beyond the themes already discussed, PKI often resulted in conversations about complexity, during deployment and operations, and connectivity risks. Notably there are alternate solutions to PKI, such as pre-shared keys, which interviewees did not mention in interviews. This focus on PKI may be indicative of interviewees not being aware of alternative solutions and a need for better communication from manufacturers. Complexity During Deployment and Provisioning Initial key provisioning requires that operators configure a certificate manager, create certificates, and deploy them to each component. Many operators expressed that they needed support from a system integrator or managed service provider for these activities. The level of support varies based on the OT protocol, with newer versions of protocols (e.g., DNP SAv2, DNP SAv5, DNP3-SL) favoring increasing automation that lessens the complexity for the end user. --- Operators should seek products that simplify the initial key provisioning, as well as system integrators that have experience setting up PKI for the selected OT protocol. Long-term, operators should seek secure discovery and provisioning capabilities that allow a certificate manager to quickly onboard new components. Complexity During Operations Field-level secure communication can operate in a responsibility gray-zone, with field components (programmable logic controllers, remote terminal units, sensors, actuators, etc.) being the responsibility of operators, and the higher-level network infrastructure and PKI being the responsibility of the security teams. This can leave operators who have no experience managing PKI in charge of key deployment and rotation. Operators found success using commercial or no-cost software that supports secure OT and general management protocols that automate their key management, prioritizing systems that are difficult to access and important to operations. Using management software also allowed for more fine-grained segmentation, with functional groupings of OT systems authenticated for communication with each other rather than treating OT as a flat network. Connectivity Risks One operator perceived PKI as requiring them to break segmentation, under the assumption that the certificate authority must be in a central site which then forces bi-directional communication from the field. Operators should balance ease of management for their system of systems with this connectivity risk. In theory, every field site could use its own certificate manager or use push-based architectures where the client initiates all key updates, trading increased complexity for reduced connectivity. PKI Usability Recommendations for Manufacturers Manufacturers can address PKI usability issues through the following practices:  Develop integrator-facing deployment guidance that enables secure communication by default. Manufacturers can reduce deployment costs by minimizing the configuration gap between legacy (brownfield) systems and new (greenfield) secure installations (e.g., standardizing interfaces, providing pre-configured templates, and offering integration support for common OT environments).  Follow Secure by Default best practices.  Ensure products have a clear design preference for secure deployment and operations. Guide the customer to that safe and secure state and away from risky operating models. Examples of risky operating models relating to secure communications include: ○ Connecting OT and IT to a central identity and access management system. ○ Creating inflexible IT dependencies for a critical engineering process. ○ Restricting inspection of operational data. --- Removing Barriers to Secure Communication Asset owners identified solutions that would lower their barriers for secure protocol adoption. Ending Proprietary Limitations Almost every asset owner referenced proprietary protocols and software as an impediment to securing their system. Some operators cited interoperability issues that locked them into a particular vendor and limited their ability to inspect traffic. The proposed solution typically involved following open standards and conformance to an assessment process. Modular Software and Hardware Several operators proposed modular hardware and software that reduces hardware costs, improves configuration exports across vendors, and makes software replacement easier without replacing the underlying hardware. Software modularity proposals were always paired with containerization technology. Containerization is common in enterprise environments and helps mitigate service downtime during updates or software errors by quickly spinning up a new software container. Available Testing Environments Secure communications protocols are developed and updated every few years. This creates an issue for customers and manufacturers, as the customer is often reluctant to adopt a new protocol, or new client software, unless a server is available to test against. Manufacturers do not frequently allocate resources to developing a server when there is no client demand, or software client available for testing. This is a circular dependency. Operators asked for clear testing infrastructure. Considerations for Post-Quantum Cryptography While this research does not directly address post-quantum cryptography (PQC), it is important to briefly discuss as a looming problem for secure communications adoption. PQC adoption in OT suffers from the same general adoption problems highlighted in this guidance. If technology is difficult to use, costly, or prone to causing downtime, then it is unlikely to be adopted. PQC raises the importance of crypto-agility, as it is likely that the PQC transition will need to occur during the lifespan of any products purchased in the 2020s. The industry will also need to pay close attention to key exchange mechanisms, as the larger key￾space will significantly increase network utilization during key exchange. Network utilization affecting system availability is already a concern, but this is likely to exacerbate the limitations of older network infrastructure and endpoints, putting more pressure on integrators and manufacturers to simplify the initial key deployment. --- Opportunity for Action The long lifecycle of OT ensures that industry will be mitigating insecure-by-design legacy protocols for decades. Each usability improvement or positive interaction with a secure protocol shortens that tail. Both critical infrastructure organizations and OT manufacturers should take the observations from operators presented in this guidance and apply them to their own infrastructure, products, and security programs. Security usability studies can take many forms, from VoC research to metrics, like tracking how many users disable security features or measuring deployment times to identify bottlenecks. Regardless of the form, operators, integrators, vendors, and manufacturers all play a role in navigating to a Secure by Design future. Conclusion Despite decades of availability, secure versions of industrial protocols remain underutilized in OT environments. CISA’s 2025 Secure by Demand for OT guidance highlights the critical need for secure communication, defined as communication with signing and/or encryption, that protects against threats like actor-in-the-middle attacks and unauthorized updates. Asset owners are motivated by ensuring the integrity and the authenticity of OT communications. However, widespread adoption of secure communications is hindered not by a lack of technical solutions but by real-world barriers in cost, complexity, and operational risk. Cost is driven by high procurement costs and licensing fees for secure-capable components and then exacerbated by complex solutions driving operators towards external assistance to deploy and maintain secure infrastructure. Complexity is increased for operators by poor integrator contracts, proprietary protocols, and unclear manufacturer guidance. Operational risk is driven by concerns over visibility, legacy infrastructure limitations, and interoperability issues. Appendix A summarizes the recommendations for operators and manufacturers to reduce these barriers. This research shows that operators desire the benefits of secure communication. Manufacturers and integrators need to factor in the usability of security to make that operator desire a reality. Acknowledgements CISA conducted this research in partnership with representatives from:  Anybus  DNP Users Group  National Security Agency  ODVA  OPC Foundation  Rockwell Automation  Schneider Electric  The Modbusaffected software product Organization  Xylem --- Appendix A. Summary of Recommendations Recommendations for Owners and Operators Owners and operators should:  Utilize signing on all communications in the OT environment and utilize encryption as needed to protect sensitive information (e.g., passwords, key exchanges, logic updates).  If concerned with limiting visibility or poor key management causing downtime, consider a phased approach beginning with signing only and not dropping packets.  Search for products which support crypto-agility, the ability to replace and adapt cryptographic algorithms, to ensure the lifetime of the product is matched by the lifetime of the cryptographic algorithm.  Seek out vendor solutions that simplify secure workflows (e.g., via management tools, wizards, system integrator support).  Ensure that open standard protocol implementations are certified, including security aspects such as key exchange mechanisms.  Prioritize secure communication in OT on remote access paths, communication between functional or network boundaries, and firmware uploads and logic changes to limit access to the OT network and mitigate the impact of malicious actors on the OT network.  Seek out products that simplify the initial key provisioning, as well as system integrators that have experience setting up security infrastructure, such as PKI, for the selected OT protocol.  Seek secure discovery and provisioning capabilities to allow a certificate manager to quickly onboard new components. --- Recommendations for OT Manufacturers Manufacturers should:  Include secure communication capabilities in OT components and protocols by default.  For integrated systems, pre-configure the system to use secure communications.  Drive out complexity to reduce costs; track KPIs associated with the usability of security features.  Maximize opportunities for asset owners to transition from legacy communication patterns.  Provide clear upgrade paths for legacy infrastructure.  Default to the secure option for all configurations, such as unique credentials, security logging, access control, communication, etc.  Ensure products have a clear design preference for secure deployment and operations; guide the customer to that safe and secure state and away from risky operating models.  Provide guidance to the customer for any required supporting infrastructure (e.g., PKI).  Develop integrator-facing deployment guidance that enables secure communication by default. ○ Manufacturers can reduce deployment costs by minimizing the configuration gap between legacy (brownfield) systems and new (greenfield) secure installations; for example, by standardizing interfaces, providing pre-configured templates, and offering integration support for common OT environments.  Build systems with cryptographic agility to remove the fear of buying at the wrong time.  Be transparent with the cost of security infrastructure.  Use open standards and interoperability testing and certification (wherever possible), increasing confidence that operations will not be disrupted. ○ In most instances, operators initially blamed the secure protocol, not the vendor, when facing interoperability challenges, which has a broad dampening effect on security.  Publish testing results that demonstrate minimum required network bandwidth for secure communications when paired with the resources of common products.

cisa.gov Central@cisa.govemail address Linkedin.com/company/cisagov @CISAgov | @cyber 1 Preparing Critical Infrastructure for Post-Quantum Cryptography Facebook.com/CISA @cisagov CISA INSIGHTS Preparing Critical Infrastructure for Post-Quantum Cryptography August 2022 Quantum Risk to Digital Communications Nation-states and private companies are actively pursuing the capabilities of quantum computers. Quantum computing opens up exciting new possibilities; however, the consequences of this new technology include threats to the current cryptographic standards. These standards ensure data confidentiality and integrity and support key elements of network security. While quantum computing technology capable of breaking public key encryption algorithms in the current standards does not yet exist, government and critical infrastructure entities—including both public and private organizations—must work together to prepare for a new post￾quantum cryptographic standard to defend against future threats. In March 2021, Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro N. Mayorkas outlined his vision for cybersecurity resilience and identified the transition to post-quantum encryption as a priority. Government and critical infrastructure organizations must take coordinated preparatory actions now to ensure a fluid migration to the new post-quantum cryptographic standard that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) will publish in 2024. Conducting an inventory of vulnerable critical infrastructure systems across the 55 National Critical Functions (NCFs) is the first step of this preparation and is included in the Post-Quantum Cryptography Roadmap developed by DHS and NIST. There are potential risks from quantum computing to each of the 55 NCFs. CISA urges asset owners and operators to follow the Roadmap and CISA’s Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative webpage to begin the process of addressing this risk within their organization. The Quantum Threat to Public Key Cryptography All digital communications—email, online banking, online messaging, etc.—rely on data encryption built into the devices and applications used to transmit and store data. This encryption is based on mathematical functions that secure data, protecting the data from tampering or espionage. In public key encryption (also known as asymmetric encryption), the mathematical functions rely on cryptographic keys to encrypt data and authenticate the sender and recipient. Public key encryption requires that each message use two separate, but related keys (one is called a public key and the other is called a private key) to protect data. The sender and recipient of the data do not share their private keys, while public keys can be shared without downgrading the level of cryptographic security. The sender uses the recipient's public key to encrypt the message and the recipient uses their private key to decrypt the message. To reply, the recipient will follow the same procedure. Similarly, digital signatures allow the sender to sign a message with their private key and the recipient to use the sender's public key to verify the integrity of the message and that the sender is actually who signed the message. All organizations regularly use public key cryptography to securely send emails, verify digital signatures, secure sensitive data, and protect user information online. When quantum computers reach higher levels of computing power and speed, they will be capable of breaking the public key cryptography algorithms that are in use today, threatening the security of business transactions, secure communications, digital signatures, and customer information. Note: Experts currently believe that quantum computers are less likely to impact symmetric key cryptography in which the sender and receiver use the same key to protect data. --- cisa.gov Central@cisa.govemail address Linkedin.com/company/cisagov @CISAgov | @cyber Facebook.com/CISA @cisagov 2 Preparing Critical Preparing Critical Infrastructure for Post Infrastructure for Post-Quantum Cryptography -Quantum Cryptography What Is Quantum Computing and How Is It a Threat? Quantum computers leverage the properties of quantum physics to derive computing capabilities that are different and, in some ways, far exceed those of classical computers. By leveraging quantum mechanics, quantum computers utilize qubits, or “quantum bits,” rather than binary bits, to achieve greater computing power and speed for specific scenarios—such as breaking current public key encryption. The algorithms that underpin the current encryption standards rely on solving mathematical problems that classical computers cannot reasonably solve. Because of their expense and physical size, quantum computers that can break encryption algorithms are likely to first be developed for use by technology companies, research institutions, or nation-states. In the hands of adversaries, sophisticated quantum computers could threaten U.S. national security if we do not begin to prepare now for the new post-quantum cryptographic standard. Potential Impacts to National Critical Functions NCFs are the functions of government and the private sector so vital to the United States that their disruption, corruption, or dysfunction would have a debilitating effect on security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or a combination thereof (see National Security Memorandum on Improving Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure Control Systems). To help critical infrastructure partners prepare for the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, CISA analyzed how each of the 55 NCFs is vulnerable to quantum computing capabilities. CISA also analyzed the challenges NCF-specific systems may face when migrating to post-quantum cryptography. The results of this analysis identified the urgent vulnerabilities and NCFs that are most important to address first to enable a successful migration to post-quantum cryptography. CISA analyzed each NCF based on its vulnerability to the expected impacts of quantum computing on the nation’s critical infrastructure. CISA ranked each NCF as high, medium, or low priority based on the urgency of its dependencies on the current cryptographic standards, the scope and scale of organizations and systems that will require updates, and the relative costs to organizations to upgrade to the new standard. CISA also ranked factors impacting each NCF’s migration as exacerbating, neutral, or mitigating. These factors include availability of human capital and status of migration preparations. Prioritizing NCFs for Stakeholder Engagement An assessment developed for CISA by the Homeland Security Operational Analysis Center (HSOAC)1 identified three NCF areas that the U.S. government and private industry should prioritize: 1 HSOAC is a federally funded research and development center operated by the RAND Corporation. 1. Several NCFs will enable the migration of most other functions to post-quantum cryptography. Success in providing this support will mitigate much of the risk for most users. 2. The dependence on industrial control systems (ICSs) is an area of concentrated vulnerability because of the long replacement life cycle of ICS hardware and wide geographic distribution of equipment. 3. NCFs with especially long secrecy lifetimes will require significant support to ensure that the nation’s most sensitive data remains fully secured. CISA will also continue to provide insight on how quantum computing capabilities impact NCFs going forward. NCFs That Will Enable Post-Quantum Migration Several NCFs will directly support the migration to post-quantum cryptography across the critical infrastructure community by providing products, patches, and other software and firmware updates that integrate the new cryptographic standard. Most NCFs and the critical infrastructure they support depend on these enabling functions to successfully execute the migration and keep their sensitive information secure. The following four NCFs are likely to be the most important in supporting successful migration: • Provide Internet-Based Content, Information, and Communication Services • Provide Identity Management and Associated Trust Support Services • Provide Information Technology Products and Services • Protect Sensitive Information CISA recommends that stakeholders responsible for these NCFs partner closely with NIST, DHS, and other government agencies to ensure their preparedness to not only migrate themselves, but also to support the --- 3 Preparing Critical Preparing Critical Infrastructure for Post Infrastructure for Post-Quantum Cryptography -Quantum Cryptography migration of digital communications across other NCFs. Action will be required of stakeholders across all NCFs, but only after these four create products and services that enable further updates to take place. Industrial Control Systems Upgrading ICSs to post-quantum cryptography will be a challenge because deployed cryptography-dependent ICS hardware is costly, and the associated equipment is often geographically dispersed. However, organizations should make necessary preparations for migration to post-quantum cryptography. CISA urges ICS organizations to ensure that their hardware replacement cycles and cybersecurity risk management strategies account for actions to address risks from quantum computing capabilities. Supporting Long Secrecy Lifetimes NCFs that depend on data confidentiality over long time frames are uniquely vulnerable to quantum challenges, including catch-and-exploit campaigns in which adversaries capture data that has been encrypted using current encryption algorithms and hold on to such data with the intention of decrypting it when a quantum computer capable of breaking the encryption is available. Organizations with a long secrecy lifetime for their data include those responsible for national security data, communications that contain personally identifiable information (PII), industrial trade secrets, personal health information (PHI), and sensitive justice system information.2 While many NCFs are potentially vulnerable to catch-and-exploit campaigns, practical challenges can inhibit adversaries from executing most campaigns successfully. For example, organizations typically store data with a long secrecy lifetime on internal networks and rarely transmit it, which limits its vulnerability. However, such security controls are not foolproof, and organizations should prioritize security for these NCFs to prevent catch-and-exploit operations. 2 Note: According to an assessment developed for CISA by HSOAC, the Operate Government NCF is “[t]o a significant degree . . . a collection of functions from other NCFs” that are included on the list, NCFs with Long-Term Confidentiality Needs. Recommended Actions for Leaders Although NIST will not publish the new post-quantum cryptographic standard until 2024, CISA urges leaders to start preparing for the migration now by following the Post-Quantum Cryptography Roadmap. Do not wait until the quantum computers are in use by our adversaries to act. Early preparations will ensure a smooth migration to the post-quantum cryptography standard once it is available. Note: Organizations should wait until the official release to implement the new standard in a production environment. NCFs that Depend on ICS • Generate Electricity • Distribute Electricity • Transmit Electricity • Transport Cargo and Passengers by Rail • Transport Cargo and Passengers by Vessel • Transport Materials by Pipeline • Transport Passengers by Mass Transit • Manage Hazardous Materials • Manage Wastewater • Store Fuel and Maintain Reserves • Exploration and Extraction of Fuels • Fuel Refining and Processing Fuels • Manufacture Equipment • Produce and Provide Agricultural Products and Services • Produce and Provide Human and Animal Food Products and Services • Produce Chemicals • Provide Metals and Materials • Supply Water NCFs with Long-Term Confidentiality Needs • Provide Internet-Based Content, Information, and Communication Services • Protect Sensitive Information • Provide Satellite Access Network Services • Support Community Health • Provide Wireless Access Network Services • Provide Information Technology Products and Services • Enforce Law • Provide Material and Operational Support to Defense • Maintain Access to Medical Records Additional Resources • CISA: Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative webpage • CISA: Prepare for a New Cryptographic Standard to Protect Against Future Quantum-Based Threats • CISA Press Release: CISA Announces Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative • RAND: Preparing for Post-Quantum Critical Infrastructure: Assessments of NCF Quantum Computing Vulnerabilities • NIST: Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography • NIST: Getting Ready for PQC: Exploring Challenges Associated with Adopting and Using PQC Algorithms • NIST: Status Report on the Third Round of NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization Process • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS): Addressing the quantum computing threat to cryptography • CCCS: Preparing your organization for the quantum threat to cryptography cisa.gov Central@cisa.govemail address Linkedin.com/company/cisagov @CISAgov | @cyber Facebook.com/CISA @cisagov

TLP:CLEARtlp classification Product ID: AA23-284A October 11, 2023 #StopRansomware: AvosLockermalware family Ransomware (Update) SUMMARY Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are releasing this joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) to disseminate known IOCs, TTPs, and detection methods associated with the AvosLockermalware family variant identified through FBI investigations as recently as May 2023. AvosLockermalware family operates under a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model. AvosLockermalware family affiliates have compromised organizations across multiple critical infrastructure sectors in the United States, affecting Windows,affected software product Linux,affected software product and VMware ESXiaffected software product environments. AvosLockermalware family affiliates compromise organizations’ networks by using legitimate software and open-source remote system administration tools. AvosLockermalware family affiliates then use exfiltration-based data extortion tactics with threats of leaking and/or publishing stolen data. This joint CSA updates the March 17, 2022, AvosLockermalware family ransomware joint CSA, Indicators of Compromise Associated with AvosLockermalware family ransomware, released by FBI and the Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). This update includes IOCs Actions to take today to mitigate cyber threats from AvosLockermalware family ransomware: • Securing remote access tools • Restricting RDP and other remote desktop services • Securing PowerShellhacking tool and/or restrict usage • Update software to latest version and apply patching updates regularly. --- FBI | CISA and TTPs not included in the previous advisory and a YARA rule FBI developed after analyzing a tool associated with an AvosLockermalware family compromise. FBI and CISA encourage critical infrastructure organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this CSA to reduce the likelihood and impact of AvosLockermalware family ransomware and other ransomware incidents. For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see: • AA23-284A STIX XML • AA23-284A STIX JSON TECHNICAL DETAILS Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework, version 13. See the MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK® tactics and techniques. For assistance with mapping malicious cyber activity to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, see CISA and MITRE ATT&CK’s Best Practices for MITRE ATT&CK Mapping and CISA’s Decider Tool. AvosLockermalware family affiliates use legitimate software and open-source tools during ransomware operations, which include exfiltration-based data extortion. Specifically, affiliates use: • Remote system administration tools—Splashtop Streamer,hacking tool Tactical RMM,hacking tool PuTTy,hacking tool AnyDesk,hacking tool PDQ Deploy,hacking tool and Atera Agent—ashacking tool backdoor access vectors [T1133].attack technique id • Scripts to execute legitimate native Windowsaffected software product tools [T1047],attack technique id such as PsExechacking tool and Nltest.hacking tool • Open-source networking tunneling tools [T1572]attack technique id Ligolo[1] and Chisel[2]. • Cobalt Strikehacking tool and Sliver[3] for command and controltactic (C2). • Lazagnehacking tool and Mimikatzhacking tool for harvesting credentials [T1555].attack technique id • FileZillahacking tool and Rclonehacking tool for data exfiltration. • Notepad++,hacking tool RDP Scanner,hacking tool and 7zip.hacking tool FBI has also observed AvosLockermalware family affiliates: 1) Use custom PowerShellhacking tool [T1059.001]attack technique id and batch (.bat) scripts [T1059.003]attack technique id for lateral movement, privilege escalation, and disabling antivirus software. 2) Upload and use custom webshells to enable network access [T1505.003].attack technique id For additional TTPs, see joint CSA Indicators of Compromise Associated with AvosLockermalware family Ransomware. NetMonitor.exefile name is a malware masquerading as a legitimate process and has the appearance of a legitimate network monitoring tool. This persistencetactic tool sends pings from the network every five minutes. The NetMonitormalware family executable is configured to use an IP address as its command server, and the program communicates with the server over port 443. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s Cross￾Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections. • Secure remote access tools by: o Implementing application controls to manage and control executiontactic of software, including allowlisting remote access programs. Application controls should prevent installation and executiontactic of portable versions of unauthorized remote access and other software. A properly configured application allowlisting solution will block any unlisted application execution.tactic Allowlisting is important because antivirus solutions may fail to detect the executiontactic of malicious portable executables when the files use any combination of compression, encryption, or obfuscation. o Applying recommendations in CISA's joint Guide to Securing Remote Access Software. • Strictly limit the use of RDP and other remote desktop services. If RDP is necessary, rigorously apply best practices, for example [CPG 2.W]: o Audit the network for systems using RDP. o Close unused RDP ports. o Enforce account lockouts after a specified number of attempts. o Apply phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA). o Log RDP login attempts. • Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions [CPG 2.N]. • Restrict the use of PowerShell,hacking tool using Group Policy, and only grant access to specific users on a case-by-case basis. Typically, only those users or administrators who manage the network or Windowsaffected software product operating systems (OSs) should be permitted to use PowerShellhacking tool [CPG 2.E]. These mitigations apply to all critical infrastructure organizations and network defenders. The FBI and CISA recommend that software manufactures incorporate secure-by￾design and -default principles and tactics into their software development practices to limit the impact of ransomware techniques (such as threat actors leveraging backdoor vulnerabilities into remote software systems), thus, strengthening the secure posture for their customers. For more information on secure by design, see CISA’s Secure by Design and Default webpage and joint guide. --- • Update Windowsaffected software product PowerShellhacking tool or PowerShellhacking tool Core to the latest version and uninstall all earlier PowerShellhacking tool versions. Logs from Windowsaffected software product PowerShellhacking tool prior to version 5.0 are either non-existent or do not record enough detail to aid in enterprise monitoring and incident response activities [CPG 1.E, 2.S, 2.T]. • Enable enhanced PowerShellhacking tool logging [CPG 2.T, 2.U]. o PowerShellhacking tool logs contain valuable data, including historical OS and registry interaction and possible TTPs of a threat actor’s PowerShellhacking tool use. o Ensure PowerShellhacking tool instances, using the latest version, have module, script block, and transcription logging enabled (enhanced logging). o The two logs that record PowerShellhacking tool activity are the PowerShellhacking tool Windowsaffected software product Event Log and the PowerShellhacking tool Operational Log. FBI and CISA recommend turning on these two Windowsaffected software product Event Logs with a retention period of at least 180 days. These logs should be checked on a regular basis to confirm whether the log data has been deleted or logging has been turned off. Set the storage size permitted for both logs to as large as possible. Configure the Windowsaffected software product Registry to require User Account Control (UAC) approval for any PsExechacking tool operations requiring administrator privileges to reduce the risk of lateral movement by PsExec.hacking tool In addition, FBI and CISA recommend network defenders apply the following mitigations to limit potential adversarial use of common system and network discovery techniques and to reduce the impact and risk of compromise by ransomware or data extortion actors: • Disable File and Printer sharing services. If these services are required, use strong passwords or Active Directory authentication. • Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drive, storage device, or the cloud). • Maintain offline backups of data, and regularly maintain backup and restoration (daily or weekly at minimum). By instituting this practice, an organization minimizes the impact of disruption to business practices as they will not be as severe and/or only have irretrievable data [CPG 2.R]. Recommend organizations follow the 3-2-1 backup strategy in which organizations have three copies of data (one copy of production data and two backup copies) on two different media such as disk and tape, with one copy kept off-site for disaster recovery. • Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service account, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST's standards for developing and managing password policies. o Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters [CPG 2.B]. o Store passwords in hashed format using industry-recognized password managers. o Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials. o Avoid reusing passwords [CPG 2.C]. o Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [CPG 2.G]. o Disable password “hints.” --- o Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year. Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring regular and frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password “patterns” cyber criminals can easily decipher. o Require administrator credentials to install software. • Require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for all services to the extent possible, particularly for webmail, virtual private networks, and accounts that access critical systems [CPG 2.H]. • Keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date. Timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats. Organizations should patch vulnerable software and hardware systems within 24 to 48 hours of vulnerability disclosure. Prioritize patching known exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems [CPG 1.E]. • Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware. Network segmentation can help prevent the spread of ransomware by controlling traffic flows between—and access to—various subnetworks, restricting further lateral movement [CPG 2.F]. • Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a networking monitoring tool. To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections, as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host [CPG 3.A]. • Install, regularly update, and enable real time detection for antivirus software on all hosts. • Disable unused ports [CPG 2.V]. • Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside your organization [CPG 2.M]. • Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [CPG 2.K, 2.L, 2.R]. VALIDATE SECURITY CONTROLS In addition to applying mitigations, FBI and CISA recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory. FBI and CISA recommend testing your existing security controls inventory to assess how they perform against the ATT&CK techniques described in this advisory. To get started: 1. Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Tables 3-7). 2. Align your security technologies against the technique. 3. Test your technologies against the technique. 4. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance. --- 5. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data. 6. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process. FBI and CISA recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory. RESOURCES • Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that gives one central location for ransomware resources and alerts. • The Joint Ransomware Guide provides preparation, prevention, and mitigation best practices as well as a ransomware response checklist. • Cyber Hygiene Services and Ransomware Readiness Assessment provide no-cost cyber hygiene and ransomware readiness assessment services. REPORTING The FBI is seeking any information that can be shared, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with AvosLockermalware family affiliates, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file. The FBI and CISA do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at ic3.gov, local FBI Field Office, or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center at report@cisa.govemail address or (888) 282-0870. Product ID: AA23-347A December 13, 2023 Co-Authored by: TLP:CLEARtlp classification Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR)threat actor group Exploiting JetBrains TeamCityaffected software product CVE Globally SUMMARY The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), U.S. National Security Agency (NSA), Polish Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW), CERT Polska (CERT.PL), and the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) assess Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR)threat actor group cyber actors—also known as Advanced Persistent Threat 29threat actor group (APT 29),threat actor group the Dukes,threat actor group CozyBear,threat actor group and NOBELIUM/Midnight Blizzard—arethreat actor group exploiting CVE-2023-42793cve identifier at a large scale, targeting servers hosting JetBrains TeamCityaffected software product software since September 2023. Software developers use TeamCityaffected software product software to manage and automate software compilation, building, testing, and releasing. If compromised, access to a TeamCityaffected software product server would provide malicious actors with access to that software developer’s source code, signing certificates, and the ability to subvert software compilation and deployment processes—access a malicious actor could further use to conduct supply chain operations.attack technique name Although the SVRthreat actor group used such access to compromise SolarWindsaffected software product and its customers in 2020, limited number and seemingly opportunistic types of victims currently identified, indicate that the SVRthreat actor group has not used the access afforded by the TeamCityaffected software product CVE in a similar manner. The SVRthreat actor group has, however, been observed using the initial accesstactic gleaned by exploiting the TeamCityaffected software product CVE to escalate its privileges, move laterally, deploy additional backdoors, and take other steps to ensure persistent and long-term access to the compromised network environments. To bring Russia’s actions to public attention, the authoring agencies are providing information on the SVR’s most recent compromise to aid organizations in conducting their own investigations and securing their networks, provide compromised entities with actionable indicators of compromise (IOCs), and empower private sector cybersecurity companies to better detect and counter the SVR’s malicious actions. The authoring agencies recommend all organizations with affected systems that did not immediately apply available patches or workarounds to assume compromise and initiate threat hunting activities using the IOCs provided in this CSA. If potential compromise is detected, administrators should apply the incident response recommendations included in this CSA and report key findings to the FBI and CISA. --- International Partnership For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see: • AA23-347A (STIX XML, 77KB) • AA23-347A (STIX JSON, 70KB) THREAT OVERVIEW SVRthreat actor group cyber operations pose a persistent threat to public and private organizations’ networks globally. Since 2013, cybersecurity companies and governments have reported on SVRthreat actor group operations targeting victim networks to steal confidential and proprietary information. A decade later, the authoring agencies can infer a long-term targeting pattern aimed at collecting, and enabling the collection of, foreign intelligence, a broad concept that for Russia encompasses information on the politics, economics, and military of foreign states; science and technology; and foreign counterintelligence. The SVRthreat actor group also conducts cyber operations targeting technology companies that enable future cyber operations. A decade ago, public reports about SVRthreat actor group cyber activity focused largely on the SVR’s spearphishingattack technique name operations, targeting government agencies, think tanks and policy analysis organizations, educational institutions, and political organizations. This category of targeting is consistent with the SVR’s responsibility to collect political intelligence, the collection of which has long been the SVR’s highest priority. For the Russian Government, political intelligence includes not only the development and executiontactic of foreign policies, but also the development and executiontactic of domestic policies and the political processes that drive them. In December 2016, the U.S. Government published a Joint Analysis Report titled “GRIZZLY STEPPE – Russian Malicious Cyber Activity,” which describes the SVR’s compromise of a U.S. political party leading up to a presidential election. The SVR’s use of spear phishingattack technique name operations are visible today in its ongoing Diplomatic Orbiter campaign, primarily targeting diplomatic agencies. In 2023, SKW and CERT.PL published a Joint Analysis Report describing tools and techniques used by the SVRthreat actor group to target embassies in dozens of countries. Less frequently, reporting on SVRthreat actor group cyber activity has addressed other aspects of the SVR’s foreign intelligence collection mission. In July 2020, U.S., U.K., and Canadian Governments jointly published an advisory revealing the SVR’s exploitation of CVEs to gain initial accesstactic to networks, and its deployment of custom malware known as WellMess,malware family WellMail,malware family and Sorefangmalware family to target organizations involved in COVID-19 vaccine development. Although not listed in the 2020 advisory, the authoring agencies can now disclose that the SVR’s WellMessmalware family campaign also targeted energy companies. Such biomedical and energy targets are consistent with the SVR’s responsibility to support the Russian economy by pursuing two categories of foreign intelligence known as economic intelligence and science and technology. In April 2021, the U.S. Government attributed a supply chain operation targeting the SolarWindsaffected software product information technology company and its customers to the SVR.threat actor group This attribution marked the discoverytactic that the SVRthreat actor group had, since at least 2018, expanded the range of its cyber operations to include the widespread targeting of information technology companies. At least some of this targeting was aimed at enabling additional cyber operations. Following this attribution, the U.S. and U.K. Governments published advisories highlighting additional SVRthreat actor group TTPs, including its exploitation of various CVEs, the --- SVR’s use of “low and slow” password sprayingattack technique name techniques to gain initial accesstactic to some victims’ networks, exploitation of a zero-day exploit, and exploitation of Microsoft 365affected software product cloud environments. In this newly attributed operation targeting networks hosting TeamCityaffected software product servers, the SVRthreat actor group demonstrably continues its practice of targeting technology companies. By choosing to exploit CVE-2023-42793,cve identifier a software development program, the authoring agencies assess the SVRthreat actor group could benefit from access to victims, particularly by allowing the threat actors to compromise the networks of dozens of software developers. JetBrains issued a patch for this CVE in mid-September 2023, limiting the SVR’s operation to the exploitation of unpatched, Internet-reachable TeamCityaffected software product servers. While the authoring agencies assess the SVRthreat actor group has not yet used its accesses to software developers to access customer networks and is likely still in the preparatory phase of its operation, having access to these companies’ networks presents the SVRthreat actor group with opportunities to enable hard-to- detect command and controltactic (C2) infrastructure. REG_DWORD /d "0" /f Adversary Toolset In the course of the TeamCityaffected software product operation, the SVRthreat actor group used multiple custom and open source available tools and backdoors. The following custom tools were observed in use during the operation: ---  GraphicalProtonmalware family is a simplistic backdoor that uses OneDrive,hacking tool Dropbox,hacking tool and randomly generated BMPs [T1027.001]attack technique id to exchange data with the SVRthreat actor group operator.  After execution,tactic GraphicalProtonmalware family gathers environment information such as active TCP/UDP connections [T1049],attack technique id running processes [T1049],attack technique id as well as user, host, and domain names [T1590].attack technique id OneDrivehacking tool is used as a primary communication channel while Dropboxhacking tool is treated as a backup channel [T1567].attack technique id API keys are hardcoded into the malware. When communicating with cloud services, GraphicalProtonmalware family generates a randomly named directory which is used to store infection-specific BMP files - with both commands and results [T1564.001].attack technique id Directory name is re-randomized each time the GraphicalProtonmalware family process is started.  BMP files that were used to exchange data were generated in the following way: 1. Compress data using zlib, 2. Encrypt data using custom algorithm, 3. Add “***” string literal to encrypted data, 4. Create a random BMP with random rectangle, 5. And finally, encode encrypted data within lower pixel bits. While the GraphicalProtonmalware family backdoor has remained mostly unchanged over the months we have been tracking it, to avoid detection the adversary wrapped the tool in various different layers of obfuscation, encryption, encoders, and stagers. Two specific variants of GraphicalProtonmalware family “packaging” are especially noteworthy – a variant that uses DLL hijackingattack technique name [T1574.002]attack technique id in Zabbixaffected software product as a means to start executiontactic (and potentially provide long-term, hard-to-detect access) and a variant that masks itself within vcperfhacking tool [T1036],attack technique id an open-source C++ build analysis tool from Microsoft.  GraphicalProtonmalware family HTTPS variant – a variant of GraphicalProtonmalware family backdoor recently introduced by the SVRthreat actor group that forgoes using cloud-based services as a C2 channel and instead relies on HTTP request. To legitimize the C2 channel, SVRthreat actor group used a re-registered expired domain set up with dummy WordPress website. Executiontactic of HTTPS variant of GraphicalProtonmalware family is split into two files – stager and encrypted binary file that contains further code. INDICATORS OF COMPROMISE Note: Please refer to Appendix B for a list of IOCs. VICTIM TYPES As a result of this latest SVRthreat actor group cyber activity, the FBI, CISA, NSA, SKW, CERT Polska, and NCSC have identified a few dozen compromised companies in the United States, Europe, Asia, and Australia, and are aware of over a hundred compromised devices though we assess this list does not represent the full set of compromised organizations. Generally, the victim types do not fit into any sort of pattern or trend, aside from having an unpatched, Internet-reachable JetBrains TeamCityaffected software product server, leading to the assessment that SVR’s exploitation of these victims’ networks was opportunistic in nature and not necessarily a targeted attack. Identified victims included: an energy trade association; companies that provide software for billing, medical devices, customer care, employee monitoring, financial management, marketing, sales, and video games; as well as hosting companies, tools manufacturers, and small and large IT companies. --- DETECTION METHODS The following rules can be used to detect activity linked to adversary activity. These rules should serve as examples and adapt to each organization’s environment and telemetry.
